text: Book 3

1. We must remember that our life is being spent every day, and less and less of it remains. But we must also consider that even if we live longer, it is uncertain whether our minds will stay sharp enough to manage our affairs or grasp the deeper knowledge of human and divine things. When old age takes hold, our breathing, digestion, imagination, and basic impulses might keep working. However, our ability to control ourselves, accurately understand our duties, analyze our senses, or even know when it is time to depart this life—all these powers that require a clear mind will fade away. So we must get up and get to work. We must do this not just because death comes closer every day, but because our understanding and intelligence often leave us before we actually die.

2. Notice the grace and charm that appear even in the unintended side effects of nature's work. For example, some parts of a loaf crack and burst open in the oven. Even though the baker didn't plan for this cracking, it looks beautiful and makes us hungry. Figs burst open when they are fully ripe, and ripe olives take on a special beauty just as they begin to rot. The drooping heads of wheat, the fierce brow of a lion, the foam at a wild boar's mouth, and many other things are not exactly beautiful on their own. Yet, because they are part of nature's process, they add to its overall beauty and bring joy to whoever looks at them. If a person is sensitive to these details and has a deep understanding of how the universe works, almost everything in nature will bring them pleasure. This kind of person will look at the real, fierce jaws of wild animals with just as much delight as they would look at a painting or sculpture of them. They will look with pure eyes at the maturity and grace of old men and women, just as they appreciate the inviting charm of youth. Many things like this will catch their attention. These details might seem unbelievable to most people, but they are obvious to anyone who is truly familiar with nature and close to its heart.

3. Hippocrates cured many diseases, but then he got sick himself and died. The Chaldeans predicted the deaths of countless people, but eventually, fate came for them too. Alexander the Great, Pompey, and Julius Caesar completely destroyed whole cities and slaughtered tens of thousands of soldiers in battle, but in the end, they also had to leave this life. Heraclitus spent his life theorizing about how the world would end in fire, but he died swollen with fluid and covered in cow dung. Parasites killed Democritus, and parasites of a different kind killed Socrates. What does all this mean? You got on the ship, you made the voyage, and now you have arrived at the port. It is time to get off. If you are stepping into another life, God will be there too. If you are stepping into nothingness, at least you will be finished with the burden of pain and pleasure. You will no longer be a slave to your physical body, which is so much weaker than the mind that serves it. Your soul is intelligence and a piece of the divine, but your body is just dust and decay.

4. Do not waste the rest of your life worrying about what other people are doing, unless it serves the common good. If you are always wondering what someone else is doing and why, or what they are saying, thinking, or planning, you are definitely neglecting your own work. All these distractions only pull you away from guarding your own mind. You must train your thoughts to avoid anything that is pointless or useless. Above all, you must avoid being overly nosy or mean-spirited. Train yourself to only think about things that you could share immediately if someone asked you. If someone suddenly asked,
What are you thinking about right now?

you should be able to answer honestly and without hesitation. Then it will be obvious that your thoughts are pure and kind, exactly as they should be for a social being who cares little for shallow pleasures or self-indulgence. You will be free from jealousy, suspicion, or any other thought that you would be embarrassed to admit. A person who decides to live this way, striving to be among the best, is like a priest or a servant of the gods. They use the spirit within them to stay untouched by cheap pleasures, unhurt by pain, and safe from insults or evil. They are a champion in the greatest contest of all: the fight to conquer every passion. This person is filled with a sense of justice and deeply accepts whatever fate brings them. They rarely worry about what someone else says or does, unless there is an urgent public need. They stay focused entirely on their own actions, while remembering their place in the grand design of the universe. They make sure their actions are good, trusting that the role they have been assigned is exactly right for them. After all, everyone's destiny is part of the universal law, and it is the law for them too. They never forget that all rational creatures are connected, and that loving all humanity is a fundamental part of human nature. They also know that we shouldn't care about what everyone thinks, but only what those who live in harmony with nature think. As for people who live differently, they always remember how those people act at home and in public, day and night, and the kind of company they keep. Because of this, they never value the praise of people who don't even respect themselves.

5. When you take action, do not do it unwillingly, selfishly, without thought, or because you feel forced. Do not dress up your thoughts with unnecessarily fancy words. Do not talk too much or stick your nose into everyone else's business. Let the divine spark within you guide you as a strong, mature person, a leader, and a dedicated citizen. Stand ready like a soldier waiting for the order to march out of this life. You should not need anyone else to swear by your character or testify to your worth. Above all, be cheerful. Do not rely on other people for your peace of mind or ask them for help. It is your duty to stand on your own two feet, rather than being propped up by others.

6. If you can find anything in this life better than justice, truth, self-control, and courage; if you can find anything better than the deep satisfaction of your own mind when it follows reason and accepts the things you cannot control—if you find anything better than this, then run to it with all your heart and enjoy it. But if nothing seems better than the divine spirit within you, which has conquered your impulses, filters your thoughts, pulls itself away from physical temptations like Socrates did, and dedicates itself to God and the love of humanity; if you find everything else to be small and worthless compared to this, then do not give your attention to anything else. Once you allow yourself to be distracted by other things, you will lose your focus on the truest good that belongs only to you. You cannot mix what is truly good and rational with things that contradict it, like the praise of the crowd, power, wealth, or the pursuit of pleasure. These things might seem acceptable for a little while, but they will quickly take over and lead you astray. So make a clear, free choice to choose the best, and stick to it. The best is whatever is truly good for you. If it benefits your spiritual side, hold onto it tightly. If it only benefits your physical body, admit it with humility and keep your choice modest. Just make sure you are judging carefully.

7. Never value anything as an advantage if it forces you to break your promises, lose your honor, or hate, suspect, or curse another person. Never value something that requires you to act fake or desire things that must be hidden behind closed doors. A person who values their soul, the divine spark within them, and the practice of true virtue above everything else does not need to put on a tragic show. They do not need to be alone, nor do they need a crowd of people around them. Best of all, they will live their life neither seeking death nor running away from it. They do not care whether their soul is housed in their body for a short time or a long time. If they had to leave this world right now, they would go as easily as they would do any other proper and decent action. The only thing they spend their entire life avoiding is allowing their mind to act in a way that is unfit for an intelligent and social being.

8. If you look into the mind of someone who has disciplined and purified themselves, you will not find anything rotten, foul, or corrupted. Fate does not cut their life off prematurely, like an actor who is pulled off the stage before their part is finished. There is nothing servile or fake about them. They are not too obsessed with social rules, but they don't isolate themselves either. They do not fear judgment, and they have nothing to hide.

9. Deeply respect your ability to form opinions. This is the only thing that keeps your mind from holding beliefs that go against your nature as a rational being. This ability is what keeps you from making rash judgments, helps you treat others with kindness, and keeps you obedient to the gods.

10. Throw away everything else and hold onto just these few rules. Remember that you only live in this exact present moment, which disappears in a flash. The rest of your time is either already gone or completely unknown. The time we have to live is very short, and the little corner of the earth we live on is very small. Even the longest-lasting fame after you die is still incredibly short. Fame is just passed down through a line of fragile mortals who will also soon die. These people do not even understand themselves, let alone someone who died a long time ago.

11. Add this rule to the others. Always define and describe whatever object or event captures your imagination. Break it down so you can see it naked, exactly as it is in its pure essence and in its entirety. Tell yourself its true name, the names of the parts that make it up, and what it will eventually break down into. Nothing expands your mind quite like the ability to carefully examine everything you encounter in life. When you look at something, think about where it fits in the universe and what its purpose is. Ask yourself why it matters to the whole world, and why it matters to a human being, who is a citizen of the highest city, a city that makes all other towns look like mere households. When something makes an impression on you, ask yourself: What is this thing made of? How long is it supposed to last? What virtue does it require from me? Does it call for gentleness, courage, honesty, loyalty, simplicity, independence, or something else? For every event, tell yourself:
This comes from God,
or
This comes from the complex weaving of fate and chance,
or
This comes from my fellow human being, my relative, or my friend.

If it comes from someone who does not know what is truly in harmony with nature, that is fine. I do know, and so I will treat them with kindness and justice, following the natural law of society. But when it comes to things that do not truly matter, I will do my best to see them for exactly what they are worth.

12. If you do your current work with a firm, eager, and kind dedication to reason; if you ignore all side-distractions and keep your inner spirit pure, as if you might have to hand it back to its creator at any moment; if you stick to this without chasing new desires or running from your fears; if you are simply satisfied with doing your natural work right now and speaking with absolute heroic honesty, then you will live well. And absolutely no one can stop you from doing this.

13. Just as a surgeon always keeps their knives and tools ready for a sudden emergency, you must always keep your principles ready. Use them to understand both human and divine things, and remember the deep connection between the two in every single thing you do, no matter how small. If you ignore this connection, you will fail in your duties to both the gods and humanity.

14. Stop wandering aimlessly. You are probably never going to re-read your own journals, the histories of the ancient Greeks and Romans, or the notes you saved for your old age. So hurry toward your true goal. Throw away your empty hopes. If you care about yourself at all, rescue yourself right now while you still can.

15. People do not really understand the deeper meaning of simple words like stealing, planting, buying, resting, or figuring out what needs to be done. You cannot see these things with your physical eyes. You need a different kind of vision to truly grasp them.

16. We have a body, a soul, and a mind. The senses belong to the body, passions belong to the soul, and principles belong to the mind. Getting distracted by the physical images around us is something we share with the animals in the field. Being tossed around by violent passions is something we share with wild beasts, weak-willed cowards, and cruel tyrants like Nero and Phalaris. Even having a mind that can point out what seems logical is something we share with atheists, traitors, and people who lock their doors to commit terrible crimes. Since all these things are common to everyone, what is left that makes a good person special? It is the ability to gladly accept everything that happens and everything that fate decides. It is the commitment to never pollute the divine spark within their heart or drown it in a flood of chaotic thoughts. Instead, they keep it peaceful and follow it like a god. They speak only the truth and act with perfect justice. And even if no one else believes they actually live such a simple, modest, and content life, they do not get angry at anyone for doubting them. They just stay on the path that leads to the true end of life, an end they will reach pure, calm, ready to leave, and completely at peace with their destiny.
End of Book 3
